title: Polynomial root coordinates before reductivity is known
statement: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional rational vector space and $R\subset V\setminus\{0\}$ a reduced crystallographic root system spanning $V$, with coroot functionals $\bar c_\alpha$ and weight lattice $P=\{v\in V:\bar c_\alpha(v)\in\mathbf Z\text{ for every }\alpha\in R\}$ in the conventions of [lem-sfb-root-datum-lattice-embedding]. Let $\mathfrak g,\mathfrak h,h_\delta,e_\alpha,\rho,W,\Omega,\Lambda$ satisfy the Chevalley-basis and faithful-representation conditions of [lem-sfb-chevalley-admissible-representation]: $\mathfrak g$ is split semisimple over $\mathbf Q$, $\rho$ is faithful on finite-dimensional $W$, the nonzero weight spaces $W_\lambda$ have weights $\Omega\subset P$ with $\mathbf Z\Omega=P$, and the full lattice $\Lambda=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Omega}(\Lambda\cap W_\lambda)$ is stable under every $D_{\alpha,m}=\rho(e_\alpha)^m/m!$, with $\rho(e_\alpha)$ nilpotent. Fix a simple-root base $\Delta$, meaning a subset $\Delta\subseteq R$ which is a basis of $V$ such that every root has integral coordinates in $\Delta$ all nonnegative or all nonpositive. Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], $W_F=\Lambda\otimes_{\mathbf Z}F$, and $T=D_F(P)=\operatorname{Spec}F[P]$, where $F[P]$ has basis $e^\lambda$, multiplication $e^\lambda e^\mu=e^{\lambda+\mu}$, comultiplication $e^\lambda\mapsto e^\lambda\otimes e^\lambda$, counit $e^\lambda\mapsto1$, and antipode $e^\lambda\mapsto e^{-\lambda}$. Embed $T$ in $\operatorname{GL}(W_F)$ by its weight characters on the summands $(\Lambda\cap W_\lambda)\otimes F$. Define the finite polynomial matrices $x_\alpha(a)=\sum_{m\geq0}(D_{\alpha,m}\otimes1)a^m$ for every commutative $F$-algebra. Group schemes and closed subgroups have the meanings of [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], and $\mathbf G_a,\mathbf G_m$ those of [def-sc-gm-ga].  Put $R^+=R\cap\sum_{\delta\in\Delta}\mathbf Z_{\geq0}\delta$, $N=|R^+|$, and fix any order on $R^+$ refining nondecreasing height (the sum of the simple-root coefficients). Write $p_+(b)=\prod_{\beta\in R^+}x_\beta(b_\beta)$ and $p_-(a)=\prod_{\beta\in R^+}x_{-\beta}(a_\beta)$, using this order. Each $p_\pm:\mathbf A_F^N\to\operatorname{GL}(W_F)$ is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion], and its image $U_\pm$ is a closed subgroup scheme. For every rational linear functional $q:V\to\mathbf Q$ strictly positive on $\Delta$ and separating the distinct weights in $\Omega$, order the weight summands by decreasing $q(\lambda)$. Then $U_+$ consists of block upper unitriangular matrices and $U_-$ of block lower unitriangular matrices, with identity diagonal blocks on the weight summands. Here block upper (respectively lower) unitriangular means identity diagonal blocks and zero blocks below (respectively above) the diagonal. The assertions are scheme-theoretic over every commutative $F$-algebra, in every characteristic, and do not assume reductivity of a generated group. When $R=\varnothing$, both images are the identity subgroup and $N=0$.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153), Theorem 23.72 and Notes, printed pp.510-511. Agent-stated supporting lemma: Closedness and uniqueness of the ordered one-sign exponential products on an admissible full-weight lattice; integral root-string collection, without an ambient reductive group.

proof.text: Use the canonical rational pairing of $V$ with $V^\vee$ for the given roots and coroots. By [lem-sfb-root-base-rational-integral-spans], the simple coroots form a rational basis and their integer span $L^\vee$ is the span of all coroots. Thus $P=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf Z}(L^\vee,\mathbf Z)$ inside $V$: integrality on the simple coroots is equivalent to integrality on all coroots. Apply [lem-sfb-root-base-reflection-induction] to the dual root pairing, with predicate that a coroot is primitive in $L^\vee$. The simple coroots are primitive since they are an integer basis; negation preserves primitivity; a simple reflection is an integral involution of $L^\vee$ and therefore preserves primitivity. These verify all three induction hypotheses. Hence every coroot is primitive, so for each $\alpha$ there is $\nu_\alpha\in P$ with $\bar c_\alpha(\nu_\alpha)=1$.

source.place: Appendix C.21-C.22, printed p.612, and C.35-C.38, pp.615-616; dual-base argument, expanded by agent.

proof.text: Choose a $\mathbf Z$-basis of each weight summand of $\Lambda$ and concatenate them. Set $E_\alpha=\rho(e_\alpha)$ and $H_\alpha=\rho(h_\alpha)$. All $E_{\pm\alpha}$ are integral and $[E_\alpha,E_{-\alpha}]=H_\alpha$; on the $\lambda$ summand $H_\alpha$ is multiplication by the integer $\bar c_\alpha(\lambda)$, by the stated Chevalley representation conditions [lem-sfb-chevalley-admissible-representation]. If $E_\alpha$ vanished modulo a prime $p$, this commutator would vanish, so every $\bar c_\alpha(\lambda)$ for $\lambda\in\Omega$ would be divisible by $p$. Since $\mathbf Z\Omega=P$, the same would hold on $P$, contradicting step 1. Therefore $E_\alpha\otimes F\ne0$ in positive characteristic. In characteristic zero this follows from faithfulness and $e_\alpha\ne0$. This applies to both signs, without any reductive group.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted details of Theorem 23.72, printed pp.510-511; agent expansion of the one-sign root-coordinate argument.

proof.text: The bracket relation with $\mathfrak h$ gives $D_{\alpha,m}W_\lambda\subseteq W_{\lambda+m\alpha}$: iterating $[h,E_\alpha]=\alpha(h)E_\alpha$ gives eigenvalue $\lambda(h)+m\alpha(h)$. Intersect with the integral weight summands and base change; thus this remains a statement about the original weight labels over every $F$-algebra, even when differentiated weights coincide. For $m>0$ and $\alpha>0$, $q(\lambda+m\alpha)>q(\lambda)$, so the associated matrix block is strictly above the diagonal in decreasing $q$ order. The term $m=0$ is the identity. Products remain block upper unitriangular because a succession of positive shifts still has positive $q$ value. Replacing every root by its negative proves the lower assertion.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted details of Theorem 23.72, printed pp.510-511; agent expansion of the one-sign root-coordinate argument.

proof.text: The divided-power multiplication identity $D_{\alpha,i}D_{\alpha,j}=\binom{i+j}{i}D_{\alpha,i+j}$ holds as an equality of integral matrices, since both sides agree over $\mathbf Q$. Comparing coefficients with the binomial theorem gives $x_\alpha(s)x_\alpha(t)=x_\alpha(s+t)$ over $\mathbf Z[s,t]$. In particular $x_\alpha(0)=1$ and $x_\alpha(s)^{-1}=x_\alpha(-s)$ after every base change. These identities also show that every factor of $p_\pm$ is invertible, so the polynomial matrices define the asserted morphisms into $\operatorname{GL}(W_F)$.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted details of Theorem 23.72, printed pp.510-511; agent expansion of the one-sign root-coordinate argument.

proof.text:
For each positive root $\beta$ choose a nonzero matrix entry $c_\beta$ of $E_\beta\otimes F$, possible by step 2, in a block from weight $\lambda$ to weight $\lambda+\beta$. In that entry of $p_+(b)$, expansion of the finite product gives
$$c_\beta b_\beta+Q_\beta((b_\gamma)_{\operatorname{ht}\gamma<\operatorname{ht}\beta}).$$
Indeed a selected monomial with exponents $m_\gamma$ shifts weight by $\sum m_\gamma\gamma=\beta$. If its total degree is one it must be the $\beta$ term, and if its total degree exceeds one, positivity of height forces every participating root to have strictly smaller height than $\beta$. Consequently $Q_\beta$ is obtained by multiplying the indicated integral matrices and retaining just these finitely many monomials; its reduction is an actual polynomial over $F$.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted details of Theorem 23.72, printed pp.510-511; agent expansion of the one-sign root-coordinate argument.

proof.text:
Recursively by height define a polynomial in the ambient matrix entries by
$$r_\beta(M)=c_\beta^{-1}\bigl(M_{i_\beta j_\beta}-Q_\beta((r_\gamma(M))_{\operatorname{ht}\gamma<\operatorname{ht}\beta})\bigr).$$
At height one the polynomial $Q_\beta$ is zero; at each larger height the right side uses only polynomials already defined. Step 5 proves by this induction that $r_\beta(p_+(b))=b_\beta$ as a polynomial identity. Thus the pullback $F[\operatorname{GL}(W_F)]\to F[b_\beta]$ contains every coordinate $b_\beta$ and is surjective. Its affine spectrum map is a closed immersion by the affine characterization in [def-weil-closed-immersion]. The identical recursion, using entries of $E_{-\beta}\otimes F$ and shifts $-\beta$, proves this for $p_-$. The constants inverted are nonzero elements of $F$, never integers assumed invertible in $F$.

source.place: Tag 01QO, lemma-closed-immersion, equivalence of (1) and (2); combined with the agent polynomial recursion above.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-chevalley-nonopposite-exponential-commutator] to two distinct roots of the chosen sign. Its hypotheses are exactly the given Chevalley basis, nilpotent representation operators and divided-power stable full lattice. Every new factor has root $i\alpha+j\beta$ with $i,j>0$, so its positive height (using $-R^+$ for the negative sign) strictly exceeds each exchanged root's height. Apply the displayed identity with $(u,v)$ replaced by $(-u,-v)$, which is allowed since it holds for all elements of every test algebra, and multiply it on the left by $x_\beta(v)x_\alpha(u)$; with step 4 this gives $$x_\alpha(u)x_\beta(v)=x_\beta(v)x_\alpha(u)\prod_{(i,j)\in S_{\alpha,\beta}}x_{i\alpha+j\beta}(c_{\alpha,\beta;i,j}(-u)^i(-v)^j).$$ Thus two adjacent factors are exchanged, and the finitely many new factors, all of strictly higher height, stand to the right of both exchanged factors. Same-root factors combine by step 4. All these are polynomial identities over every test algebra.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted details of Theorem 23.72, printed pp.510-511; agent expansion of the one-sign root-coordinate argument.

proof.text: Collect any finite word of one sign by ascending height. Inductively, the word has a prefix containing the already collected roots of heights less than $h$ in the specified order, followed by factors of height at least $h$. Move the finitely many height-$h$ factors to the front of that tail in the specified order, using step 7, and combine equal roots. Each exchange creates only factors of height greater than $h$, so it creates no new height-$h$ factor; moving each of the finitely many such factors across the finite intervening word terminates. The resulting tail has height greater than $h$. The initial prefix is empty at $h=1$, and after the maximal root height there is no tail. This proves the induction and produces an ordered product with polynomial parameters. Apply it to the concatenation of two ordered products and to the reversed word with negated parameters. Both multiplication and inverse therefore preserve the image on every $F$-algebra, including algebras with nilpotents.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted details of Theorem 23.72, printed pp.510-511; agent expansion of the one-sign root-coordinate argument.

proof.text: By step 6 the image $U_\pm$ is the closed subscheme identified with $\mathbf A_F^N$ by $p_\pm$. Its points over an arbitrary $F$-algebra are exactly the uniquely parametrized ordered products, because a closed immersion is an isomorphism onto its closed image. Step 8 and the zero tuple show that these subsets contain the identity and are closed under products and inverses. This is precisely the closed-subgroup criterion in [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]; the polynomial collected parameters give its structure morphisms, and their group identities follow from the injective matrix realization. Together with step 3 this proves every assertion scheme-theoretically.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted details of Theorem 23.72, printed pp.510-511; agent expansion of the one-sign root-coordinate argument.

proof.text: If $R=\varnothing$, then $N=0$ and both products are empty products equal to the identity. The source is $\operatorname{Spec}F$ and the identity subgroup is closed by the equations $M_{ij}=\delta_{ij}$ in the general-linear coordinate algebra; its block diagonal is the identity. The arguments for nonempty $R$ used no restriction on the characteristic, on nilpotents in a test algebra, or on the chosen height-refining order.

The spans lemma makes the simple coroots a basis of the coroot lattice L^vee, and reflection induction on the dual pairing holds (simple coroots are a basis, negation and integral reflections preserve primitivity). Since P = Hom(L^vee, Z), each coroot takes value 1 on some element of P. (2) If E_alpha were 0 mod p, then H_alpha = [E_alpha, E_-alpha] would be 0 mod p, so the coroot would be divisible by p on Omega and hence on Z Omega = P, contradicting step 1. (3) Weight shifts and decreasing-q order give the triangularity. (4) Additivity of x_alpha comes from the binomial identity for divided powers. (5)-(6) Height recursion: degree-2 monomials only involve lower heights, giving retractions r_beta, so the pullback is surjective and def-weil-closed-immersion gives a closed immersion. (7) FAULT, repaired: multiplying the commutator identity by x_beta(v)x_alpha(u) gives x_a x_b = C x_b x_a, which puts the new higher factors to the left and breaks the step-8 collection invariant. The FIX substitutes (-u,-v) and left-multiplies, giving x_a(u)x_b(v) = x_b(v)x_a(u) times the product of x_{ia+jb}(c(-u)^i(-v)^j), with the new factors on the right. (8) With that, collection by height terminates. (9) The closed-subgroup criterion of def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup holds. (10) R empty is handled.
